stories.headline: Earthquake of magnitude 6.1 strikes off Kanto coast, tsunami forecast issued for slight sea level changes
stories.title: Earthquake of magnitude 6.1 strikes off Kanto coast, tsunami forecast issued for slight sea level changes
stories.summary: New Delhi [India], November 6 : An earthquake measuring 6.1 on the Richter scale struck the North Pacific Ocean, off the eastern coast of the Kanto region, on Friday afternoon, according to the National Centre for Seismology (NCS). The seismic event was recorded at 4:09 PM IST on Friday, about 145 km from Choshi, Chiba, Japan. According to data released by the NCS, the earthquake originated at a relatively shallow depth of 40 kilometres beneath the surface. The epicentre of the tremor was located at latitude 35.087° N and longitude 142.254° E. "EQ of M: 6.1, On: 06/11/2026 16:09:29 IST, Lat: 35.087 N, Long: 142.254 E, Depth: 40 Km, Location: North Pacific Ocean," NCS posted on X. Meanwhile, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) has issued a tsunami forecast following the earthquake off the eastern coast of the Kanto region. While no major tsunami warning, tsunami warning, or tsunami advisory has been triggered, the JMA’s forecast highlights potential minor sea-level fluctuations along the eastern Kanto coastline. Authorities do not expect destructive waves, but coastal residents and maritime operators are urged to remain attentive and follow official updates. Further details regarding potential impacts, felt intensities, or damage are currently awaited. Earlier in August, an earthquake with a magnitude of 6.0 struck parts of the northern Japanese prefecture of Hokkaido on Sunday evening, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA), making it the second quake that hit Japan today. The epicentre of the quake was recorded off Hokkaido at a depth of 40 kilometres at 10:45 pm (local time). The seismic intensity scale was 4 out of a maximum of 7, as per JMA, which said that no tsunami warning was issued. Earlier this morning, an earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 5.9 hit the eastern region of the country, leaving over 40 people injured in Tokyo and neighbouring prefectures, authorities said, as per the official Kyodo News Agency. The tremor prompted a warning by the weather agency about similar quakes in the coming days. The 2:00 am (local time) quake had originated in the southern part of Ibaraki Prefecture at a depth of 68 kilometres and registered lower 5 on the Japanese seismic intensity scale of 7 in parts of the prefecture as well as in central Tokyo, the official media said. The morning quake was felt across a wide swath of the country, including northeastern and central Japan. The earthquake triggered delays for early morning train operations, while several services were compelled to proceed at reduced speeds, according to JR East and regional transit operators. According to the recorded parameters, the epicentre was located approximately 125 kilometres south of Obihiro and 36 kilometres south-southeast of Urakawa. Local authorities are monitoring the situation following the seismic event. Kyodo News noted that a lower 5 quake is defined by the agency as shaking that causes most people to be frightened and to hold on to something stable, while objects may fall from shelves. In the morning quake, transportation was impacted following the event. The start of some train services was delayed, while some trains ran at reduced speeds, according to JR East and other operators, as cited by Kyodo News. Furthermore, some express services operated by Tobu Railway remained halted. Following the early morning earthquake, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi announced that the government has established an emergency response task force at the PMO to assess the situation. (ANI)

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Friday (November 6) pronounced judgment on a Miscellaneous Application filed by the Centre seeking clarification of its March 11 judgment holding that the creamy layer status of an Other Backward Class (OBC) candidate cannot be determined solely on the basis of the parents' salary income, and that the category of posts held by them has also to be considered.
The Court clarified that the judgment was applicable to the parties before the Court and that seniority and promotions would not be reopened.
The pending cases will be decided by the courts on their own merits and entitlement.
The time to comply with the judgment was extended by eight weeks.
A bench of Justice Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha and Justice R. Mahadevan pronounced the judgment on a Miscellaneous Application filed by the Centre seeking prospective application of the judgment.
A copy of the judgment is awaited.

“Retrospective or belated application of a changed eligibility criterion may unsettle appointments and admissions made under the rules and certificates prevailing at the relevant time and may create uncertainty regarding OBC-NCL status, seniority, service conditions and career progression.
It may also affect admissions to Central and State educational institutions, universities and professional institutions.

The Applicant therefore respectfully submits that the temporal operation of the Judgment requires clarification so as to avoid unsettling completed selections, appointments and admissions and the consequential rights arising therefrom”, the plea states.

The Centre had sought two years to establish equivalence of posts in other organisations with government posts after consultations with the concerned stakeholders and to formulate a uniform mechanism for determining OBC creamy-layer status where equivalence has not been established.

The Centre had also sought permission to finalise service allocation for 958 candidates recommended by the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) in the Civil Services Examination (CSE) 2025, pending a decision on the clarification application.
By the March 11 judgment, the Supreme Court held that salary income alone cannot determine whether a candidate belongs to the OBC creamy layer.

stories.headline: LTCG cut buzz turns spotlight on India's valuation premium
stories.title: LTCG cut buzz turns spotlight on India's valuation premium
stories.summary: The growing chatter around a potential cut in equity long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax has shifted attention to a deeper market debate among investors—whether India is trying to attract foreign investors with tax incentives at a time its valuations remain a hurdle. While a friendlier tax regime could improve returns at the margin, many investors argue that foreign institutional investors (FIIs) allocations are driven far more by earnings prospects and relative valuations.“No tax change has turned a falling market. Removal would raise the response of flows to a rising market, not create the rise,” says Venkatesh Balasubramaniam, managing director and head of research, JM Financial. He insists that lower taxes are not enough to attract more foreign investors to India. “Tax matters at the margin and as a signal, but it cannot by itself bring FIIs back,” he says further, adding that tax relief could fetch an estimated $3–5 billion in foreign institutional investors (FIIs) inflows by FY28.India taxes FIIs like any other category of investors—at 20 percent on short-term gains and 12.5 percent on long-term gains—while most Asian markets impose no capital gains tax at all. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) has recommended removing LTCG tax for FIIs and easing tax treatment for mutual fund scheme switches, though the final decision rests with the Centre, a Reuters report said. The proposals come amid continued foreign outflows from Indian equities and follow discussions in which overseas investors flagged taxation as a key concern.Also Read: Indian stock market running on oppressed, caged capitalFIIs have been consistently dumping Indian stocks over the last few months, so much so that only domestic institutional investors (DIIs), including mutual funds, banks and pension funds, have provided valuable support to the overall markets.In October, FIIs sold $2.2 billion worth of equities taking their net outflows for the year to $30.4 billion. DIIs, meanwhile, remained net buyers, investing $6.3 billion in October, taking their cumulative equity inflows to $74.1 billion in the year so far.Meanwhile, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said at a media event that the government is mindful of investor concerns over high valuations and capital gains taxes but cautioned that tax incentives alone do not drive market performance. Ahead of the Union Budget likely to be presented on February 1, Sitharaman said the government would consider stakeholder feedback before taking any decision.“Against the current backdrop of sustained foreign investor selling, elevated global yields and capital moving towards competing markets, revisiting LTCG taxation may be timely,” says Hitesh Sawhney, partner, Price Waterhouse & Co LLP.He explains that a nil tax rate on long-term capital gains, linked to a relatively longer holding period, could reward patient capital, encourage investors to remain invested in India and strengthen India’s relative capital market attractiveness. “It would also reduce foreign investors’ dependence on treaty-based exemptions and the resulting uncertainty over treaty eligibility,” he adds.However, if India's growth prospects and corporate fundamentals remain attractive, why should foreign capital require an additional nudge?Vishal Lohia, partner, Dhruva Advisors, says the reported recommendation by Sebi to reconsider the LTCG tax for FIIs is a constructive step towards enhancing the global competitiveness of Indian equities. However, when analysing recent FPI outflows, it is helpful to view the headline tax rate as one component of a broader macroeconomic and regulatory ecosystem, rather than the singular driver of capital movement.“Historically, while taxes are a critical consideration for foreign allocators, they do not act in isolation. Several mature global markets command premium capital despite carrying a high combined capital gains tax burden. article_sentences: It is particularly unfortunate that a dispute remained pending for several decades, the Court commented.

The Supreme Court on Friday directed the States of Punjab and Haryana to supply approximately 11,973 million units (MU) of electricity to Himachal Pradesh over a period of 20 years, thereby bringing to a close a decades-long dispute over the sharing of power generated from the Bhakra-Nangal and Beas hydroelectric projects.

A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana directed the two States to supply the power arrears at the rate of approximately 598 million units per annum during the lean seasons (October to March).
The Court also directed that Himachal Pradesh's liability towards its 7.19% share of the capital cost of the projects, assessed at ₹420.77 crores, be adjusted against the energy arrears.
For this purpose, the electricity shall be valued at ₹3.85 per unit, resulting in an adjustment of approximately 1,093 million units.

The directions were issued in a suit instituted by Himachal Pradesh in 1996 under Article 131 of the Constitution, seeking its rightful share in the electricity generated from the two hydroelectric projects.
The Court had, in its 2011 judgment, declared Himachal Pradesh entitled to 7.19% of the power attributable to the erstwhile composite State of Punjab.
However, the implementation of the decree led to further disputes concerning the quantum of arrears, the applicable tariff and the capital-cost liabilities of the States.
The Union of India had computed Himachal Pradesh's total energy arrears at 13,066 million units for the period from November 1, 1966, until October 2011.
It proposed that the arrears be supplied in kind over 15 years, with the capital-cost liability being adjusted against the energy entitlement.

Punjab disputed the computation, contending that the arrears should be reduced after accounting for the additional power supplied to Himachal Pradesh and that the capital-cost liability should be calculated differently.
Haryana also raised objections concerning the quantum of its liability.

stories.headline: How the Vaziranis built Saffronart into much more than an auction house
stories.title: How the Vaziranis built Saffronart into much more than an auction house
stories.summary: In April, when a 19th-century Raja Ravi Varma painting titled Yashoda and Krishna was sold for a record-setting ₹167.2 crore ($17.9 million) at an auction in Delhi—becoming the most expensive Indian artwork ever sold—it grabbed headlines and attention within and outside India. The sale also brought to the fore the rising demand for art among Indian collectors who are pushing prices to never-known-before highs. Varma’s painting was bought by Cyrus Poonawalla, founder and managing director of Serum Institute of India.The artwork was auctioned by Mumbai-based Saffronart, which was co-founded by Minal and Dinesh Vazirani and turned 25 last year. The April auction symbolised not just the evolution of the art market in India, but also the journey of Saffronart, which the Vaziranis had started with the sole purpose of making the buying and selling of art more transparent and accessible.As young collectors in 1994—when Minal and Dinesh got married and returned to India from the US—the couple would spend their weekends visiting art galleries and museums, browsing through exhibitions and collections, and buying pieces for their personal collection. “I had joined my family business, which is into manufacturing cranes and other heavy equipment, while Minal was working with Andersen Consulting and Accenture,” says Dinesh, who studied for a bachelor’s degree in fine art and a master’s in industrial engineering at Stanford University. “And, in all our free time, we used to go to galleries and museums and just look at art.”Also Read: Indian art market sees dip in sales, but high-priced pieces buck trendSaffronart, he explains, was born more from their frustration as collectors. “We had relationships with only a few galleries. We used to visit them and they would pull out a few paintings one by one, and most of these paintings were ones they hadn’t offered to their best clients. There was a hierarchy there. For a young collector, there was very little avenue to get the best works.” Adding to this hierarchy was the fact that there were hardly any publications on art at that time, there was nothing on the internet, there was no price transparency, and there was no way to compare what the price of an artwork should be. Dinesh and Minal Vazirani, co-founders, Saffronart. Photo by Swapnil Sakhare for Forbes India“At that time, you could go to a couple of different galleries, see two different works by an artist, from a similar period, and find a price difference of as much as 30 to 40 percent,” says Minal. “And it wasn’t just about the quality of the work— because that does play a big role—there wasn’t as much information out there about pricing. There was no mal intent on the part of the galleries. But to see such a price difference for artworks that were so similar was something we didn’t understand.”As young collectors, they didn’t intend to start a business in the art space initially, recalls Minal. “The way it happened is, I was solving a very personal problem that we were facing. And that was basically, if we wanted to buy art, how do you figure out how much to pay for it and where do you acquire it from, and get what would be one of the best works of an artist.”What the Vaziranis wanted was a platform where they had all the information available, and it was a democratic platform where everyone had the same level of access. “An auction seemed like the most democratic process,” says Dinesh.Consequently, when Minal wrote the business plan for Saffronart—she had a BS in chemical engineering and bioengineering with a minor in art history and Indian history from the University of California, Los Angeles—transparency was a key pillar. The second pillar was to provide access to the best artworks. She recalls one of her classes while studying for an MBA at Insead in France, where the professor had said, “When you’re starting off a business plan and as you ideate, what is it that you want to wake up in the morning and do every day? What is it that would excite you to wake up every day? Because you have got to work through it.” “And,” Minal says, “I thought, well, this is what I do for fun on weekends. And of course, I’d love to wake up every day and do this. And that’s how I began designing the business.” (Clockwise from top left) Dinesh with Tyeb Mehta; Dinesh with Jehangir Nicholson and Sharan Apparao; Minal with SH Raza; Minal and Dinesh with Krishen Khanna and Kiran Nadar; Dinesh with Ebrahim Alkazi. Taking off, and crashingAs the Vaziranis got Saffronart off the ground in 2000, there were limited resources. Hence, the only way to reach potential and existing collectors, showcase the artworks, make the information available and create an environment for collectors to engage with and acquire the works was to do everything online. “It seemed like the natural way to go,” recalls Minal.They went to galleries to source artworks from them, compiled an online catalogue and put the artworks online. The first auction included small works of Modern Indian artists such as MF Husain and SH Raza. “We became an aggregator. We got access to a lot of different artworks at the same time. And we published prices, which the galleries were horrified with. Because there was always closed-doors pricing for art; there was no openness,” recalls Dinesh. He remembers the resistance they faced, especially from the industry itself. “People said, ‘who’s going to buy art online? You’re silly, what are you doing?’” he adds.If there was one part of the industry that didn’t want a disruptive newcomer, there were others who supported them. “They said, ‘You’re growing the market, so it’s positive’. It is the support of those which we appreciate even today and respect,” says Dinesh.Minal and he were firm on their belief that art is fundamentally an image, and worked to add more information to that image so that people get comfortable with online purchases. Buttressing the photographs of artworks were closeups shots (with the ability to zoom in and out) and videos, information about the condition of the artwork and related research. “We tried to replicate online the same characteristics that were there in the physical world to make the decision easier for people. We did our first auction at the end of 2000, in November. It was a two-week online auction, which seemed to last forever,” laughs Dinesh, comparing them to the 24-hour online auctions that are now common.Minal and Dinesh had waited with bated breath, waiting for bids to come in. The online did well, resulting in $100,000 of sales. But what caught them off guard was when, around the same time, someone in New York bought around 20 other artworks worth $25,000 that were listed on the website. They wondered if there had been a mistake and called up the buyer. Turned out the buyer was designer Nayeem Khan. “When we asked him what made him spend that amount of money, he simply said, ‘It was just so easy for me, sitting in New York, to get access to art, to know it’s going to be shipped to my door’,” remembers Dinesh, talking about how Khan helped them navigate the logistics process of shipping the artworks. “We had to work with the likes of DHL, FedEx and Blue Dart to help gear their systems towards packaging and shipping art, since it is a specialised product,” he says.Minal says one of the cornerstones of Saffronart is being as good or better than anyone else in the market. “And I don’t mean that flippantly. I’m thinking back to the first catalogue that we printed. We reprinted it three times, because I didn’t want to hear what I’d heard earlier, which was, ‘Oh, it’s really good for an Indian company’. Nothing annoyed me more,’” she recalls. “I just want someone to look at it and say, this is fantastic. I don’t think geography has anything to do with it. I don’t think the constraints we are working with have anything to do with it. It’s just that I want to be superlative.”Since internet penetration and the concept of buying things online were in their nascency in India at that time, Dinesh and Minal began to look to other markets, with mature internet ecosystems, in which to find buyers. “In India, we were still trying to upload data on those dial-up modems. And just as you were about to upload the whole file, it would crash,” says Dinesh. They decided on going to markets where, one, art formed a cultural bridge and access was much more important for people living outside India, and, two, they were used to the internet.Also Read: Indians have gotten used to buying art online: Saffronart CEOBut since no one knew Saffronart, it had to build credibility among prospective buyers. Subsequently, over the next few years, Saffronart organised largescale international shows in cities with large Indian diaspora such as New York, San Francisco, Hong Kong and London. “We did those shows between 2001 and 2003, but the market wasn’t growing,” says Dinesh.By 2003, Dinesh and Minal were left looking at a business that was not making money to sustain itself. “We looked at the numbers and had to ask ourselves, ‘Should we shut this down?’,” remembers Dinesh. “But as entrepreneurs, you always have the feeling that you don’t want to fail. We took loans, we sold our personal art collection to fund the company. We gave it one last push, and all the work we had put in to convince people that we have a credible platform suddenly fit like a jigsaw in 2004.”Saffronart had raised institutional funding initially from what became ChrysCapital, and, over time, as both their businesses changed, they parted ways. “We got to a point in 2003 where we almost shut down, and we had to pull our socks up and make this company work,” adds Minal. “And if we hadn’t pushed, we wouldn’t have survived that year. It helped that we had each other to lean on. Dinesh and I did that really well for each other as co-founders, as business partners. And it made a big difference to be able to have a partner whose decision-making you trust implicitly.” First live auctionRebuilding and successSaffronart completed 25 years late last year. It is an auction house that has become synonymous with not just high-value auctions (see For the Record), but one of the significant players in the Indian art market that has been instrumental in building the ecosystem.“What Minal and Dinesh saw was a great opportunity and a void in the art space, where you had all these international auction houses that were looking at India, but from a huge distance. A Christie’s or a Sotheby’s are not homegrown brands,” says Kishore Singh, veteran art writer and curator. “They came in with their own international learnings. They brought that skill set to organising and creating Saffronart. They launched the first professional auction model in the country, and the first auction house that went online. They widened access and reach. These were people who created, I think the term that I would like to use is, a great sense of affection for Indian arts.”Singh elaborates that Saffronart curated their auctions in ways that would draw buyers into the process, and make them eager to participate. The way in which the catalogues were done, for instance, were meant to incentivise buyers—they would begin with very attractive names like Jamini Roy, with sales typically beginning at low price points, and then move gradually to higher price points as buyers went through the catalogue. “The website was brilliantly conceived in design, and the fact that they announced auctions and kept to the schedule meant you had four opportunities to look forward to,” says Singh. “In terms of management, administration and organisation, they did that brilliantly.”Validating Singh’s views, Minal says that two factors that have been critical for the success of Saffronart are in-house expertise and professionalism. “We brought in people with knowledge, and leveraged their expertise. When we were speaking of transparency, it’s not just of price but also of information. It’s presenting information about artists and their careers about which you couldn’t just go online and find. It simply wasn’t there,” she says. “We have had a very low rate of attrition within our team, because the team here was involved in building something that no one had ever done before. There was a sense of ownership and being part of that story of growth.”The other thing that was very important to her was to bring in a level of professionalism, which meant being transparent with clients, providing a level of service that they haven’t had in this space, in this part of the world, being direct, and having integrity.Most importantly, though, Dinesh and Minal both concur that Saffronart succeeded because of perseverance—which they were compelled to demonstrate early in their journeys as entrepreneurs—and innovation. “As we began growing, that’s really where the innovation came in. It was doing things that had never been done before,” says Minal. “This idea of innovating, to create something, is what really excited me about breaking new ground, about experimenting with this business in a way that hadn’t been done before,” she adds. “It was extraordinarily difficult, which brings me to the point that Dinesh brought up about perseverance.”While technology has been one of the largest elements of innovation, it has not been the only one. “We evaluate a great deal of technology in the background, even if we don’t roll it out. We evaluate not only how it affects Saffronart, but the art market at large. We try and take responsible decisions about whatever we put out there,” says Minal. “It goes without saying that AI-enabled technologies are sort of a way forward on many fronts. And, of course, that’s something we’re evaluating. We use a bit of it already.”But, Minal adds, innovation comes in different forms. One of the things she believes they have done is make innovation the engine of growth not just for Saffronart but the overall ecosystem, which has given the market a great deal of depth and breadth in terms of collectors, driving transaction values and volume.“We rolled out Story Ltd [in 2013] in order to do no-reserve auctions. This was a fallout of what had happened during the global financial crisis [in 2008] and the terror attacks in Mumbai. It had been a period that was extraordinarily difficult economically. We had postponed our auctions for a few months. Values had dropped. We had galleries coming up to us; one gallery in particular said, ‘We haven’t sold anything for a few months. I’m not able to pay salaries. Here’s my inventory, sell it for whatever you can get for.’ And it really was difficult to sell.” Art Mumbai, a modern and contemporary art fair founded by Dinesh and Minal Vazirani, along with other art professionals, showcases artworks from South Asia and across the worldSaffronart began no-reserve auctions, both as a technological and a market innovation, because it allowed a small reset of prices in a transparent and professional manner, where the market was allowed to decide the price points. “Obviously, it had guardrails, but that was incredible. And we’ve continued doing that. And it’s allowed for innovation in terms of extending the offering of what can come into auction. It has also enabled first-time buyers by removing the intimidation that sometimes surrounds a high-level auction,” says Minal.The most recent addition to the ecosystem has been Art Mumbai, a modern and contemporary art fair showcasing artworks from South Asia and across the world. Founded in 2023, the fair is a gathering of leading Indian and international galleries, artists, collectors, curators, institutions, and thought leaders. The 2026 edition—scheduled for November 12 to 15 at Mahalaxmi Race Course in Mumbai—will host 73 Indian and 21 international galleries.The fair has been instrumental in taking art, artists and artworks out of the confines of galleries and auction houses, which can often be intimidating for first-time collectors and new enthusiasts, and presenting them as an experience that combines walks, performances, musical presentations and cultural programming. Visitors can listen, walk, discover, encounter and participate, rather than simply look at art on gallery walls. The fair has seen the participation of the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art (KNMA) as well as the Saffronart Foundation from the inaugural edition, thus opening up larger conversations around the role of private and independent foundations in shaping India’s cultural ecosystem, museum access and making art more accessible to wider audiences.Summarising the work that Saffronart does, Minal says, “We’re in the business of providing access to scarcity. I mean that statement, and it’s a bit problematic. But the art we offer for sale, the collectibles that we curate and put together, those are unique, typically rare, difficult to obtain. Every collectible is a slice of history that someone feels tied to. Fact is, South Asia, and the subcontinent in particular, is a treasure trove. As a new nation, we haven’t really been able to bring it to the forefront in the same way that Western countries have done with their art. But I think what we’re doing now—and I hope what Saffronart is able to do—is build that pedestal for our own art.”

They went to galleries to source artworks from them, compiled an online catalogue and put the artworks online.
The first auction included small works of Modern Indian artists such as MF Husain and SH Raza.
“We became an aggregator.
We got access to a lot of different artworks at the same time.
And we published prices, which the galleries were horrified with.
Because there was always closed-doors pricing for art; there was no openness,” recalls Dinesh.
He remembers the resistance they faced, especially from the industry itself.
“People said, ‘who’s going to buy art online?
You’re silly, what are you doing?’” he adds.
If there was one part of the industry that didn’t want a disruptive newcomer, there were others who supported them.
“They said, ‘You’re growing the market, so it’s positive’.
It is the support of those which we appreciate even today and respect,” says Dinesh.
Minal and he were firm on their belief that art is fundamentally an image, and worked to add more information to that image so that people get comfortable with online purchases.
Buttressing the photographs of artworks were closeups shots (with the ability to zoom in and out) and videos, information about the condition of the artwork and related research.
“We tried to replicate online the same characteristics that were there in the physical world to make the decision easier for people.
We did our first auction at the end of 2000, in November.
It was a two-week online auction, which seemed to last forever,” laughs Dinesh, comparing them to the 24-hour online auctions that are now common.
Minal and Dinesh had waited with bated breath, waiting for bids to come in.
The online did well, resulting in $100,000 of sales.
But what caught them off guard was when, around the same time, someone in New York bought around 20 other artworks worth $25,000 that were listed on the website.
They wondered if there had been a mistake and called up the buyer.
Turned out the buyer was designer Nayeem Khan.

“When we asked him what made him spend that amount of money, he simply said, ‘It was just so easy for me, sitting in New York, to get access to art, to know it’s going to be shipped to my door’,” remembers Dinesh, talking about how Khan helped them navigate the logistics process of shipping the artworks.
“We had to work with the likes of DHL, FedEx and Blue Dart to help gear their systems towards packaging and shipping art, since it is a specialised product,” he says.
Minal says one of the cornerstones of Saffronart is being as good or better than anyone else in the market.
“And I don’t mean that flippantly.
I’m thinking back to the first catalogue that we printed.
We reprinted it three times, because I didn’t want to hear what I’d heard earlier, which was, ‘Oh, it’s really good for an Indian company’.
Nothing annoyed me more,’” she recalls.
“I just want someone to look at it and say, this is fantastic.
I don’t think geography has anything to do with it.

It’s just that I want to be superlative.” Since internet penetration and the concept of buying things online were in their nascency in India at that time, Dinesh and Minal began to look to other markets, with mature internet ecosystems, in which to find buyers.
“In India, we were still trying to upload data on those dial-up modems.
And just as you were about to upload the whole file, it would crash,” says Dinesh.
They decided on going to markets where, one, art formed a cultural bridge and access was much more important for people living outside India, and, two, they were used to the internet..
Subsequently, over the next few years, Saffronart organised largescale international shows in cities with large Indian diaspora such as New York, San Francisco, Hong Kong and London.
“We did those shows between 2001 and 2003, but the market wasn’t growing,” says Dinesh.
By 2003, Dinesh and Minal were left looking at a business that was not making money to sustain itself.
“We looked at the numbers and had to ask ourselves, ‘Should we shut this down?’,” remembers Dinesh.
“But as entrepreneurs, you always have the feeling that you don’t want to fail.
We took loans, we sold our personal art collection to fund the company.

We gave it one last push, and all the work we had put in to convince people that we have a credible platform suddenly fit like a jigsaw in 2004.” Saffronart had raised institutional funding initially from what became ChrysCapital, and, over time, as both their businesses changed, they parted ways.
“We got to a point in 2003 where we almost shut down, and we had to pull our socks up and make this company work,” adds Minal.
“And if we hadn’t pushed, we wouldn’t have survived that year.
It helped that we had each other to lean on.
Dinesh and I did that really well for each other as co-founders, as business partners.
And it made a big difference to be able to have a partner whose decision-making you trust implicitly.” First live auctionRebuilding and successSaffronart completed 25 years late last year.

It is an auction house that has become synonymous with not just high-value auctions (see For the Record), but one of the significant players in the Indian art market that has been instrumental in building the ecosystem.
“What Minal and Dinesh saw was a great opportunity and a void in the art space, where you had all these international auction houses that were looking at India, but from a huge distance.
A Christie’s or a Sotheby’s are not homegrown brands,” says Kishore Singh, veteran art writer and curator.
“They came in with their own international learnings.
They brought that skill set to organising and creating Saffronart.
They launched the first professional auction model in the country, and the first auction house that went online.
They widened access and reach.

These were people who created, I think the term that I would like to use is, a great sense of affection for Indian arts.” Singh elaborates that Saffronart curated their auctions in ways that would draw buyers into the process, and make them eager to participate.

The way in which the catalogues were done, for instance, were meant to incentivise buyers—they would begin with very attractive names like Jamini Roy, with sales typically beginning at low price points, and then move gradually to higher price points as buyers went through the catalogue.
“The website was brilliantly conceived in design, and the fact that they announced auctions and kept to the schedule meant you had four opportunities to look forward to,” says Singh.

“In terms of management, administration and organisation, they did that brilliantly.” Validating Singh’s views, Minal says that two factors that have been critical for the success of Saffronart are in-house expertise and professionalism.
“We brought in people with knowledge, and leveraged their expertise.
When we were speaking of transparency, it’s not just of price but also of information.
It’s presenting information about artists and their careers about which you couldn’t just go online and find.
It simply wasn’t there,” she says.
“We have had a very low rate of attrition within our team, because the team here was involved in building something that no one had ever done before.

There was a sense of ownership and being part of that story of growth.” The other thing that was very important to her was to bring in a level of professionalism, which meant being transparent with clients, providing a level of service that they haven’t had in this space, in this part of the world, being direct, and having integrity.

Most importantly, though, Dinesh and Minal both concur that Saffronart succeeded because of perseverance—which they were compelled to demonstrate early in their journeys as entrepreneurs—and innovation.
“As we began growing, that’s really where the innovation came in.
It was doing things that had never been done before,” says Minal.
“This idea of innovating, to create something, is what really excited me about breaking new ground, about experimenting with this business in a way that hadn’t been done before,” she adds.

“It was extraordinarily difficult, which brings me to the point that Dinesh brought up about perseverance.” While technology has been one of the largest elements of innovation, it has not been the only one.
“We evaluate a great deal of technology in the background, even if we don’t roll it out.
We evaluate not only how it affects Saffronart, but the art market at large.
We try and take responsible decisions about whatever we put out there,” says Minal.
“It goes without saying that AI-enabled technologies are sort of a way forward on many fronts.
And, of course, that’s something we’re evaluating.
We use a bit of it already.” But, Minal adds, innovation comes in different forms.

One of the things she believes they have done is make innovation the engine of growth not just for Saffronart but the overall ecosystem, which has given the market a great deal of depth and breadth in terms of collectors, driving transaction values and volume.
“We rolled out Story Ltd [in 2013] in order to do no-reserve auctions.
This was a fallout of what had happened during the global financial crisis [in 2008] and the terror attacks in Mumbai.
It had been a period that was extraordinarily difficult economically.
We had postponed our auctions for a few months.
Values had dropped.
We had galleries coming up to us; one gallery in particular said, ‘We haven’t sold anything for a few months.
I’m not able to pay salaries.

Here’s my inventory, sell it for whatever you can get for.’ And it really was difficult to sell.” Art Mumbai, a modern and contemporary art fair founded by Dinesh and Minal Vazirani, along with other art professionals, showcases artworks from South Asia and across the worldSaffronart began no-reserve auctions, both as a technological and a market innovation, because it allowed a small reset of prices in a transparent and professional manner, where the market was allowed to decide the price points.
“Obviously, it had guardrails, but that was incredible.
And we’ve continued doing that.
And it’s allowed for innovation in terms of extending the offering of what can come into auction.
It has also enabled first-time buyers by removing the intimidation that sometimes surrounds a high-level auction,” says Minal.
The most recent addition to the ecosystem has been Art Mumbai, a modern and contemporary art fair showcasing artworks from South Asia and across the world.
Founded in 2023, the fair is a gathering of leading Indian and international galleries, artists, collectors, curators, institutions, and thought leaders.
The 2026 edition—scheduled for November 12 to 15 at Mahalaxmi Race Course in Mumbai—will host 73 Indian and 21 international galleries.

The fair has been instrumental in taking art, artists and artworks out of the confines of galleries and auction houses, which can often be intimidating for first-time collectors and new enthusiasts, and presenting them as an experience that combines walks, performances, musical presentations and cultural programming.
Visitors can listen, walk, discover, encounter and participate, rather than simply look at art on gallery walls.

The fair has seen the participation of the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art (KNMA) as well as the Saffronart Foundation from the inaugural edition, thus opening up larger conversations around the role of private and independent foundations in shaping India’s cultural ecosystem, museum access and making art more accessible to wider audiences.
Summarising the work that Saffronart does, Minal says, “We’re in the business of providing access to scarcity.
I mean that statement, and it’s a bit problematic.
But the art we offer for sale, the collectibles that we curate and put together, those are unique, typically rare, difficult to obtain.
Every collectible is a slice of history that someone feels tied to.
Fact is, South Asia, and the subcontinent in particular, is a treasure trove.
As a new nation, we haven’t really been able to bring it to the forefront in the same way that Western countries have done with their art.
But I think what we’re doing now—and I hope what Saffronart is able to do—is build that pedestal for our own art.”
